lesson.title: The Simplest Fork: Run It or Skip It
lesson.summary: The if statement is the most basic conditional statement in Python, running one indented block when its boolean expression is True and simply skipping it otherwise, with no alternative path required.
lesson.body:
The if statement is the smallest, most direct implementation of a conditional statement. Its shape in Python is exactly: the keyword if, a boolean expression, a colon, and one or more indented lines that make up the body. There is no requirement for anything else to follow. If the expression evaluates to True, Python executes the indented body. If the expression evaluates to False, Python skips the entire body and moves on to the next statement at the original indentation level, as if the if block were not there at all. That "skip and move on" behavior is what makes the if statement the simplest possible conditional: it has exactly one path that might or might not run, and no built-in alternative.

Consider this short piece of code:

balance = 40
if balance < 50:
    print("Low balance warning")
print("Balance check complete")

Python first evaluates balance < 50. Since balance is 40, and 40 is indeed less than 50, the expression is True. Because it is True, Python runs the indented print("Low balance warning") line. Execution then continues to print("Balance check complete"), which is outside the if block and therefore always runs, regardless of the balance. Now imagine balance had been 100 instead. The condition balance < 50 would evaluate to False, the indented print would never execute, and the program would go straight from evaluating the condition to printing "Balance check complete." Nothing else changes about the program's structure, only which lines actually ran.

This example highlights the defining property of a bare if statement: it can only add behavior, never provide a substitute behavior. If you need something specific to happen when the condition is False as well, a plain if statement cannot express that on its own, you either need a second, independent if statement checking the opposite condition, or you need the if-else statement, which pairs an alternative block directly with the original condition. Choosing between "just an if" and "if paired with else" is really a question about your requirements: does the False case need to do anything at all, or is skipping enough?

The if statement also illustrates why indentation matters so much in Python. There is no explicit end keyword or closing brace marking where the body of the if statement stops, the indentation itself is the only signal. Every line indented consistently under the if line is part of its body; the first line that returns to the original indentation level is understood to be outside the if statement, back in the surrounding sequential flow. Getting this indentation right is not a stylistic preference, it changes which statements are conditional and which are not.

The condition itself can be as simple as a single boolean variable or as involved as a compound expression built from comparisons and logical operators, following the same precedence rules covered for order of operations. Something like if balance < 50 and not is_frozen: is still just one if statement, evaluating one overall boolean expression, even though that expression happens to combine two smaller conditions with and. The if statement does not care how complicated the expression is, only what single True or False value it ultimately produces.
